title: Useful work
hookLine: William Morris: useful work carries hope; useless toil does not (1884)

cards: All work is good. Hard work is its own reward. Keep busy.
Lines like these can sound like wisdom. William Morris, an English designer, craftsman and writer, wasn't so sure.

In a lecture called Useful Work versus Useless Toil, he pointed out that the people most eager to praise all labor were often the ones living on someone else's. Then he drew a line through the middle of the word work.
On one side, work worth doing. On the other, toil that only wears a person down. Today's word is the side he wanted: useful work.

teach.b: First, his test. Morris says, in paraphrase, that worthwhile work carries hope in it, and useless toil carries none. So the question isn't whether you're busy.
It's whether there's any hope in what you're doing. Second, he names three hopes.
Hope of rest: that the work ends, and the rest is real. Hope of product: that what you make is worth having, useful or beautiful, not junk made to be thrown away.
And hope of pleasure in the work itself: that the doing, not only the finishing, has something in it for the worker. In that third hope, a listener may hear an echo of Ruskin, yesterday.
Third, what toil looks like: work with none of those hopes. Endless, so rest never comes. Pointless, so nothing good is made.
Joyless, so the hours are only endured. Morris wanted a society to look hard at how much of its work fell on that side of the line, and to ask how much of it could be cut. Fourth, the small version.
Morris wrote about whole economies, but his hopes fit inside a day: a to-do list can hold a report nobody reads, a form filled in twice. His lecture doesn't tell anyone to quit a job.
It hands over a question to ask of any task: is there rest at the end of this, is the result worth having, and is there anything in the doing?
If the answer is no, three times, maybe it can go.

how: Morris's lecture Useful Work versus Useless Toil is read by students of design, craft and social thought, and his three hopes of rest, product and pleasure are cited in discussions of meaningful work.

o: work that earns the most money for the hours spent
work that keeps a person busy from dawn to dusk
work with hope of rest, a worthy product and pleasure

games.q: Morris's three hopes — tap the pairs.
p: the work ends, rest is real
work with no hope in it

s: Morris says all work is good in itself
he challenged that idea and separated useful work from useless toil.
Morris names hope of rest, of product, and of pleasure in the work
worthwhile work, he said, carries hope.
Morris's lecture tells people to quit their jobs
it offers a test for any task, not an instruction to quit.

games.q: you're William Morris. someone tells you hard work is always noble. what do you say?
o: agree: all labor is good in itself.
split it: useful work carries hope, useless toil doesn't.
say all work is a burden to escape.
games.why: Morris drew a line through the word work: on one side work full of hope, on the other toil that only wears people down.

practice: Let this week's tasks pass one by one, like cards, and ask Morris's three questions lightly of each: rest at the end, a result worth having, anything in the doing?

Notice the one task that fails all three, and hold it while you breathe, wondering whether it could be dropped, shrunk or handed back. If you pray, you can bring the choice into your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Useful work. William Morris's name for work that carries hope: of rest, of a product worth having, and of pleasure in the doing. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: pleasure in the work itself. Busy isn't the test; hope is. See you tomorrow.
